ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness | St. Louis, MO
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in St. Louis, MO: UT thickness surveys on terminal tanks and plant piping plus weld inspection, at your site. Request a UT quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in St. Louis, Missouri
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out ultrasonic testing in St. Louis, Missouri, and across the river in the Illinois metro-east: thickness surveys on terminal tanks, plant piping and vessels, and shear-wave examination of welds in fabricated steel. Technicians travel to your terminal, plant or shop, work to a written procedure and report against the code named in your contract. Request a UT inspection quote for your St. Louis site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in St. Louis

St. Louis was built on the Mississippi, and the working river still shapes what gets inspected. The city port authority manages roughly nineteen miles of riverfront and about 130 harbor facilities that move on the order of fifteen to eighteen million tons of cargo a year, and the bi-state harbor extends to America's Central Port at Granite City, Illinois, with access to six Class I railroads. Six interstate gas pipelines and nine refined-product pipelines converge on the region, and the Wood River refinery sits across the river in Illinois. Behind the docks and pipelines are chemical and detergent plants, breweries, pharmaceutical makers, aircraft and vehicle manufacturers, nonferrous foundries and metal fabricators.

For ultrasonic work, that adds up to a distinctive list of components:

  • Shell courses and floor plates of storage tanks at terminals handling liquid fertilizer, fuels and chemicals along the riverfront.
  • Pump station and metering piping where pipelines enter the region, including elbows, tees and low points that collect water.
  • Barge-loading spouts, conveyor frames and dock cranes, where thickness loss from weather and spillage weakens structural members.
  • Stainless tanks and jacketed vessels at breweries and food plants, which are thin-walled and sensitive to measurement error.
  • Process piping at chemical and detergent plants, where acids, alkalis and steam attack carbon steel from the inside.
  • Welded structural assemblies at fabrication shops, where groove welds are examined for internal fusion defects.

What ultrasonic testing can and cannot tell you

Ultrasonic testing works by timing sound. A transducer couples a pulse into the part, and the instrument displays echoes from the far wall and from anything in between. If the part is the right material and the sound velocity is known, the time to the back wall converts to thickness, and an echo from the middle of a weld reveals a reflector. No other field method looks through the wall and into the weld volume with the same economy.

Its blind spots are well understood. Corrosion pits narrower than the probe can read as a deeper back wall than the true minimum, which is why mapping or repeated scans are used where pitting is expected. A thick coating can be measured through only with a technique that has been shown to work on it. Austenitic stainless and cast components scatter sound. A crack aligned with the beam reflects little energy, so welds are scanned from several directions. And thin parts near the dead zone of a standard probe need a specialized probe. Each of these is a procedure decision, not an afterthought.

Measuring thickness on terminal tanks and plant piping

On a storage tank, the usual job is to take thickness at marked points on each shell course, on the roof where access is safe, and on accessible floor plates where the owner's tank inspection plan calls for it. The technician calibrates on a step block of tank steel, uses a dual-element probe so pitted plate still gives a readable signal, and records the minimum found at each point. These measurements feed the corrosion rate and remaining life that the owner's authorized inspector calculates under API 653.

On piping, readings are taken at condition monitoring locations on elbows, reducers, tees, dead legs and injection points, which are the places most exposed to flow-accelerated wear and water drop-out. For hot service the technician switches to a high-temperature probe and applies a temperature correction. The principal references are ASTM E797 for contact thickness measurement, the SE-797 practice in Article 23 of ASME Section V, and Article 5 of Section V for ultrasonic examination of materials; our guide to ASME Section V Article 5 covers the details.

Repeatability: grids, survey history and trend

A single thickness number is a snapshot; the value comes from repeating it. On St. Louis terminal and plant assets, the technician lays out a grid on the first survey, stamps or paint-marks each point and sketches its position against a fixed reference such as a nozzle or weld seam. The next survey, perhaps two or five years later, reads the same points with the same probe type and the same calibration approach, and the difference between the two readings is the metal that was lost in between.

That history matters more than any single reading. Short-term and long-term corrosion rates can differ sharply after a process change, a new feedstock or a coating failure, and the owner's inspector uses both. Where earlier survey data exists, we ask for it, so the new readings can be compared point for point and any location that has accelerated is flagged in the report summary instead of buried in a table.

Shear-wave examination of welds

When the question is inside the weld, the technician replaces the thickness probe with an angle-beam probe. A 45-degree beam reaches the root of a thick butt weld, a 70-degree beam suits thin plate, and 60 degrees is the common middle choice. Sensitivity is set from a reference reflector such as a side-drilled hole, and the transducer is scanned along the weld on both sides. Indications are classified by length, amplitude and position, and the acceptance table from the governing code decides whether each one is accepted.

The document that applies depends on the product. For pressure equipment, ASME Section V Article 4 gives the technique and ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 gives the acceptance standards. For process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.6 applies. For structural steel, AWS D1.1 Clause 8 in its 2020 edition covers ultrasonic examination of groove welds. A welded repair on a barge-loading structure or a crane runway usually follows the structural rules. Confirming the right document is the first task on any weld job.

Missouri rules, owner-inspector regimes and the river

Missouri's Division of Fire Safety runs the boiler and pressure vessel safety program authorized by RSMo 650.200 through 650.295. Covered objects need a valid certificate of inspection, typically renewed on a two-year cycle, and responsibility for obtaining it rests with the owner. New equipment must carry ASME construction and National Board registration. Insurers inspect what they insure; the Division inspects equipment without a carrier. Thickness data from an outside contractor helps those inspectors but does not replace their authority.

For in-service tanks, vessels and piping, API 653, API 510 and API 570 put the owner's authorized inspector in charge, with Atlantis supplying readings and indications. Plants covered by OSHA process safety management must keep mechanical integrity records under 29 CFR 1910.119(j), and pipelines fall under PHMSA's 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195. A job on the Illinois bank of the river is governed by Illinois law, so the owner's inspector confirms which jurisdiction applies before the work is scheduled.

People, procedures and reports

Technicians work under Atlantis's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the work and interprets the readings. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report; the company's Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based scheme, so the employer certifies its own technicians, and a careful buyer asks to read the written practice.

A St. Louis thickness report carries the asset tag, drawing or line number, instrument and probe, calibration block and temperature, then a table or sketch of readings with the minimum per location and any change since the last survey. A weld report names the procedure and revision, the scan plan, each recordable indication with location, length and amplitude, and an accept or reject against the named table. The ultimate UT guide goes through the method step by step.

Planning an ultrasonic job in St. Louis

River cities are humid, and St. Louis adds hot summers and winters that regularly drop below freezing. Cold slows couplant and makes it stiff, so the procedure should name a low-temperature couplant for winter tank and pipe-rack work, and equipment stored in a truck needs time to settle. Summer sun can push a steel roof or shell well above comfortable touch temperature, and the same hot surface that wears out gloves also calls for high-temperature probes. Riverfront sites can be restricted during high water, and barge schedules can limit dock access, so confirm access windows early.

Atlantis has no office in St. Louis. Technicians travel to your site, and travel for the agreed scope is part of the quotation. At terminals expect transportation worker credentials or site orientation; at chemical plants expect hot work, confined-space and lockout rules to be handled by the owner. Send the tag list, material, nominal thickness, access and code, and we will quote from it.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in St. Louis

The method follows the question. For remaining wall, or a flaw inside a weld, use ultrasonic testing. For a surface crack in carbon steel at a weld toe or lifting lug, magnetic particle inspection in St. Louis is quicker. For stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals, use dye penetrant testing in St. Louis. Repairs often combine them: a surface method on the excavation and ultrasonic testing on the finished weld. The national ultrasonic testing service page lists the full scope.

Training in-house ultrasonic technicians

Employers that want their own UT staff can send them through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, practice with the ultrasonic simulator and see the St. Louis training page for how employer-led practical hours are handled. Your company certifies the technicians it trains under its own written practice, and our written practice development service can prepare that document.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in St. Louis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in St. Louis. Technicians travel to your terminal, plant or shop for the agreed scope, and the quotation includes that travel. The work follows a written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III.

faq.q: Can you measure tank shell thickness at a St. Louis terminal?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians take thickness at marked points on each shell course and accessible floor plates, using a dual-element probe calibrated on tank steel. The owner's authorized inspector uses the minimums to set the corrosion rate and remaining life under API 653.

faq.q: How does ultrasonic testing deal with pitted steel?
faq.a: Dual-element probes and an A-scan display help, because the technician can see whether a reading reflects a true back wall. Where pitting is widespread, repeated scans or a grid with extra points are used, and the report records the lowest reading found.

faq.q: Can UT inspect welds on a dock crane or barge-loading structure?
faq.a: Yes, if the joints are accessible and thick enough for the procedure. The owner or engineer names the code, usually AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and the technician scans the weld with angle-beam probes and reports against its acceptance table.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing suitable for stainless brewery tanks?
faq.a: For wall thickness, yes, using a probe and calibration suited to thin stainless and with care that couplant is food-safe and fully cleaned off. Weld examination in thin stainless is limited, so surface methods and visual checks usually do that job.

faq.q: What do I need to arrange before a UT visit in St. Louis?
faq.a: Arrange safe access to every test point, a surface clear of loose scale and flaking coatings, the tag list or drawings, and site entry credentials. For riverfront sites confirm dock access windows and any restrictions during high water.

faq.q: Does the Illinois side of the river follow different rules?
faq.a: Yes. Missouri's rules apply to Missouri objects, and Illinois law governs equipment in Illinois. The owner's inspector or insurer confirms which state's boiler and pressure vessel rules and inspection cycle apply before the job is scheduled.

faq.q: What does a UT report from Atlantis include?
faq.a: The asset, procedure and revision, instrument, probe, calibration block, temperature, technician and level, readings or indications with locations, minimums per location and, for welds, an accept or reject against the named code table.

faq.q: How can I request a UT quote in St. Louis?
faq.a: Use the quote form with the asset list, material, nominal thickness, access, code and preferred dates. We reply within one business day with scope, procedure and quotation.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in St. Louis, MO | MPI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) in St. Louis, MO for cranes, castings, press frames and terminal steel, performed at your site. Request a quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in St. Louis, Missouri
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection in St. Louis, Missouri, on ferromagnetic steel: crane and hoist structure, river-terminal equipment, welds and repair excavations, ferrous castings and the heavy tooling used in vehicle and metal plants. Technicians are mobilized with yokes, particles and light meters, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request an MPI quote for your St. Louis site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in St. Louis

St. Louis lifts, loads and presses a great deal of steel. The riverfront harbor handles bulk cargo with cranes, conveyors and barge-loading structures; rail yards and rail-served industrial parks sit on both banks; and the regional economy includes aircraft and vehicle manufacturing, ferrous and nonferrous foundries, and metal fabrication. Presses, forklifts, hoists and cranes cycle load thousands of times, and cycling loads open surface cracks at welds, fillets and holes. That is the damage magnetic particle inspection is built to find.

Common MT jobs in this market include:

  • Crane rails, runway girders, trolley frames and hook blocks at terminals and plants, examined at welds and attachment points.
  • Barge-loading spouts, conveyor supports and dock structure where repairs have been welded.
  • Ferrous castings and forgings, such as housings, brackets and valve bodies, checked for hot tears, laps and shrinkage cracks that reach the surface.
  • Press frames, die holders and heavy tooling at vehicle and metal-forming plants.
  • Vessel and tank welds in carbon steel, including nozzle welds and temporary attachment scars after removal.
  • Structural steel erection welds on buildings and bridge repairs across the metro area.

How the method works, and where it stops

A magnetized steel part holds its field inside the metal until something disturbs it. A crack at the surface, or a few thousandths of an inch beneath it, pushes some of that field into the air. Iron particles dusted or sprayed on the part collect where the field escapes, drawing a bright line along the flaw. Because the part itself carries the field, only ferromagnetic material responds: carbon steel, most low-alloy steel and cast iron. Aluminum, copper, brass and austenitic stainless steel do not, so nonferrous foundry products need penetrant testing instead.

Depth is the main constraint. Indications fade quickly as a flaw sits deeper, and the method cannot size a flaw in depth or measure wall thickness. Direction is the second constraint. The field must cross the crack, so each area is examined with the field in two directions at roughly right angles. Finally, some patterns are not cracks at all: the edge of a weld cap, a change in hardness and a section change can each trap particles, so interpretation matters.

Examining castings, forgings and heavy fabrications

Ferrous castings from a St. Louis foundry or a repair shop are among the most rewarding MT jobs. Casting surfaces are rough, which scatters particles, and shapes are irregular, which makes field direction hard to plan. The usual answer is a combination of techniques: an electromagnetic yoke on accessible surfaces, prods or a coil on heavier sections, and a central conductor on bores and hollow parts. Wet fluorescent suspension handles the rough surface better than dry powder.

Heavy fabrications raise a different problem, which is size. A crane trolley frame or a press crown is too large to magnetize as a whole, so the examination moves along it in overlapping sections with the yoke pole spacing and the overlap recorded. Technicians mark each position so a later reader can reproduce the pattern, and they note where access or geometry prevented a full examination so the owner knows exactly what was covered.

Technique and equipment

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the lifting-power test for yokes: an alternating-current yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing in use, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. Technicians check this with a calibrated test weight before work and again at the intervals in the procedure. Field strength is also confirmed with a pie gauge or a shim-type indicator on the first piece, so the setup is shown to reveal a known flaw before real work begins.

Wet fluorescent work is done under UV-A light in a darkened area, with a light meter confirming intensity and the white-light level at the surface. Contrasting powders, applied dry in a light cloud, suit outdoor field welds and warm surfaces. Afterward, parts that will be machined, welded or fitted with sensitive bearings may need to be demagnetized, and a field meter confirms the residual level. The Article 7 requirements explained page describes each requirement in plain language.

Weld repairs and crack removal

Magnetic particle inspection is the standard check around a repair. When a crack is found in a crane girder or a tank attachment, the metal is ground out and the excavation is examined to show that the crack is gone before welding resumes. After the repair weld is made and dressed, the area is examined again, and the report ties each result to the repair record. This sequence keeps a hidden crack tip from being welded over, which is how a small defect becomes a repeat failure.

Preheat and post-weld heat treatment can affect timing. Steel that has been preheated may be too warm for wet particles, while a part that has just been stress relieved needs to cool to the temperature range of the procedure. Technicians coordinate with the welder so that the examination happens when the surface is ready, and so that the weld is not covered, painted or insulated before it has been checked.

Lifting equipment and fatigue programs

Cranes, hoists and rigging at terminals and plants are often covered by a periodic inspection program written by the owner or its insurer. Those programs name critical welds and components, such as hook shanks, trolley frames, boom pivots and runway splices, and set an interval for magnetic particle examination. Atlantis performs that examination as a defined scope, records the position of each examined area and reports any indication to the owner's competent person, who decides whether the equipment remains in service.

The same approach works for press frames and heavy tooling in vehicle and metal-forming plants. A baseline examination on a healthy machine gives later examiners a reference, and the report shows where cracks started in past service. Recording the location of each examined weld and the technique used lets the next examination repeat the work exactly, which is the most reliable way to catch crack growth between intervals.

Codes and Missouri context

The technique references are ASME Section V Article 7, ASTM E1444 and the guide ASTM E709. Acceptance comes from the construction code in the contract: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for state bridge work. Where API 510, API 570 or API 653 governs, the owner's authorized inspector directs the inspection and Atlantis reports the indications.

In Missouri the Division of Fire Safety enforces the boiler and pressure vessel law, and certificate inspections of covered equipment are the owner's responsibility. Equipment on the Illinois side is covered by Illinois rules. Lifting equipment, including cranes, falls under OSHA requirements and the owner's own program, which often names MT of critical welds at set intervals.

Reports and who stands behind them

The technician is a Level II qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The procedure is approved and the report reviewed by an ASNT Level III, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Because SNT-TC-1A makes the employer the certifying party, a buyer should ask any contractor for its written practice.

An MT report names the component and its ID, the procedure and revision, the equipment with its calibration or lifting-power check date, the particle type and color, light readings for fluorescent work, field-strength verification, the technician and level, and the surface condition. Indications are located by sketch or photograph with length and orientation, and each is accepted or rejected against the named criteria.

Planning an MPI job in St. Louis

St. Louis has a continental climate, with cold, damp winters and hot, humid summers. Cold surfaces slow the carrier in wet suspensions and chill the technician's hands, so winter work may require a shelter or heater, and condensation on cold steel is cleared before particles are applied. In summer, steel in direct sun can run hot enough to dry particles before they migrate to the flaw, so shading or a procedure for elevated temperature is needed. Riverfront wind can blow dry powder away, which is a good reason to use wet methods outdoors.

Atlantis has no office in St. Louis, so crews travel to the site; the quotation covers the agreed scope and travel. Terminal and plant sites bring their own entry, safety and lockout procedures, and owners arrange scaffolds, lifts, and surface preparation. Let us know the component list, material, access and code in your request.

MT, PT or UT for your St. Louis project

Carbon steel with a possible surface crack: magnetic particle testing. A non-magnetic casting or stainless weld: dye penetrant testing in St. Louis. A concern about wall loss or internal weld quality: ultrasonic testing in St. Louis. The MT versus PT comparison helps decide, and the national magnetic particle testing page lists the full scope.

Training your own MT staff

Companies that qualify their own technicians can start with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, read the complete MT guide and check eligibility with the SNT-TC-1A eligibility tool. The St. Louis training page explains the course and the employer practical.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in St. Louis for MPI work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in St. Louis. Crews are mobilized to your site with their own yokes, particles and light meters, and the quotation covers the agreed scope and travel.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on nonferrous castings?
faq.a: No. Aluminum, brass, copper and austenitic stainless castings cannot be magnetized, so magnetic particle testing does not work on them. Dye penetrant testing is the surface method for those materials.

faq.q: How do you inspect a large casting or press frame?
faq.a: The technician examines in overlapping sections with a yoke, prods or a coil, records pole positions and overlap, and notes any areas that geometry prevented from being covered. Each section is examined in two field directions.

faq.q: What is a yoke lifting-power test?
faq.a: It shows that a yoke produces enough field. ASME Section V Article 7 requires at least 10 pounds of lift for an alternating-current yoke and 40 pounds for direct-current or permanent-magnet yokes at the largest pole spacing used.

faq.q: Is fluorescent MPI better than dry powder?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles are more sensitive and handle rough surfaces better, but need UV-A light and a dark area. Dry powder is easier outdoors and on warm steel. The procedure and code decide which is appropriate for a given job.

faq.q: Do I have to demagnetize parts after MPI?
faq.a: Only when residual magnetism would interfere with welding, machining, bearings or nearby instruments. The procedure says when it is required and how the residual field is verified, and the report records whether it was done.

faq.q: Can you inspect crane rails and lifting gear at a terminal?
faq.a: Yes, where access and safety are arranged by the owner. Technicians examine welds, attachment points and hardware on carbon steel and report cracks with location and size against your specification.

faq.q: What does an MPI report contain?
faq.a: The component ID, procedure and revision, equipment and verification dates, particle type, light readings, technician and level, surface condition, and each indication with a sketch, length, orientation and accept or reject decision.

faq.q: How do I request MPI service in St. Louis?
faq.a: Use the quote form to send the component list, material, access conditions, governing code and preferred dates. We reply within one business day with a scope and a written quotation for your site.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Testing in St. Louis, MO | PT Inspection
pt.description: Dye penetrant testing in St. Louis, MO for castings, stainless welds and process equipment, performed at your plant or shop. Request a PT quote today.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in St. Louis, Missouri
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing in St. Louis, Missouri: dye penetrant inspection of castings, welds and machined parts in aluminum, stainless steel, nickel alloys and other non-porous metals where a surface-breaking crack must be found. Technicians are mobilized to your plant or shop, work from a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a penetrant testing quote for your St. Louis site and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in St. Louis

The St. Louis region has a long history of metalworking, and the freight-and-industry freight summary for the region lists metals, chemicals, detergents, beverages, pharmaceuticals and aerospace among its areas of concentration. Nonferrous foundries serve the vehicle sector. Chemical and detergent plants rely on stainless steel and nickel alloy equipment. Breweries and pharmaceutical makers run polished stainless vessels and piping. Each of these industries has parts for which a magnet is useless, and penetrant is the dependable surface method.

Typical PT work in St. Louis:

  • Aluminum and magnesium castings and machined housings, checked for shrinkage cracks, hot tears and porosity open to the surface.
  • Stainless and nickel-alloy welds on reactors, heat exchangers and process piping at chemical and detergent plants.
  • Brewery and pharmaceutical tank, jacket and piping welds on polished stainless equipment.
  • Repair welds on pumps, valves and rotating equipment where a crack was ground out and must be proven clean.
  • Machined shafts, fittings and fasteners in brass, bronze and stainless that see cyclic loading.
  • Weld preparation faces and root passes on small-bore alloy pipe.

What dye penetrant can and cannot show

Liquid penetrant testing depends on capillary action. A thin liquid, left on a clean surface for a set time, creeps into any opening to the surface. Once the excess is cleaned off, a developer draws the trapped liquid back out and spreads it, enlarging a hairline crack into a clear line. The method needs no electricity and no magnetization, works on almost any non-porous solid and gives results that an examiner can read directly.

The same mechanism sets the limits. The flaw has to be open to the surface, so a buried defect of any size will not be detected. A surface that has been peened, smeared or sealed by grinding or blasting can hide a crack, and porous surfaces hold penetrant and produce a haze that obscures real indications. Penetrant also tells nothing about depth, so a recorded crack is sized by length at the surface and its depth, if needed, is found by another method, such as ultrasonic testing, or by excavation.

Foundry castings and rough surfaces

Castings are the hardest penetrant subject and the one where a skilled examiner earns their pay. As-cast surfaces are rough and porous in places; machined faces are smooth; and cracks and porosity cluster at section changes, corners and gating locations. On an aluminum casting, fluorescent penetrant under UV-A light is usual because it reveals fine cracks in an uneven surface. Water-washable systems clean up rough surfaces more easily than solvent systems, and the washing step needs close control to avoid washing penetrant out of real indications.

Scattered round indications from porosity must be separated from linear indications from cracks, because the acceptance rules treat them differently. The technician photographs patterns and records both the location and the number of indications in a reference area. Rework after a rejection is common on castings, so the report should state how re-examination will be done and what happens if a casting is repaired by welding.

Process control: cleaning, dwell, removal and development

The procedure sets each step. Cleaning removes oil, paint and scale, and the surface is dried so no solvent or water remains in a flaw. Penetrant is applied and left for its dwell time, long enough to fill fine cracks and not so long that it dries on the surface. Excess is removed with the method suited to the system, and the surface is dried. Developer is applied in a thin, even coat and the part is examined within the time window the procedure gives.

Controls extend beyond the part. Temperature must be within the range the procedure was qualified for, and ASME Section V Article 6 uses 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit as the standard range. Fluorescent systems need a black-light intensity check and a dark area. Penetrant and developer lots are recorded, and for austenitic stainless and nickel alloys the materials carry certifications for low halogen and sulfur content. Residues are cleaned off after the examination.

Proving repairs on pumps, valves and process equipment

A frequent penetrant job is the check after a repair. A cracked pump casing, valve body or vessel nozzle is ground out, and penetrant testing of the excavation shows whether any trace of crack remains before the weld is made. After welding and dressing, the repaired area is examined again. Because the same material may have been welded before, the technician checks the surrounding heat-affected zone as well as the weld itself, since cracks often run along the fusion line.

The sequence needs careful scheduling. Penetrant residues must not be left in an excavation that will be welded, so the area is cleaned thoroughly after each examination. Preheated areas must cool into the qualified temperature range before testing, and the technician coordinates with the welder to avoid delays. The report ties the penetrant results to the repair record and the material, so the owner has a complete file for the equipment.

Fluorescent examination and the dark area

Fluorescent penetrant is the most sensitive version of the method, and it places demands on the examination environment. The technician needs a UV-A source whose intensity at the surface is verified with a meter, and a darkened area where white light does not wash out the glow. In a shop, that may be a portable booth or a corner screened with curtains. Outdoors, it usually means working at night or under a tent, and on a sunny St. Louis summer day the shade needed can be larger than expected.

The examiner also needs a minute or two of dark adaptation before reading indications, and eyewear that does not fluoresce. Indications fade, so photographs are taken early. Many owners ask for fluorescent examination on castings, where fine cracks in rough surfaces would be missed under white light, and for critical rotating parts, where a small crack can grow into a failure.

Records for plants with their own quality systems

Chemical, brewing and pharmaceutical plants in the metro area keep their own quality records, and an outside inspector's report becomes part of the equipment history. Atlantis formats its penetrant reports so that a quality group can file them without rework: the equipment tag, the weld numbers examined, the procedure and revision, the materials with lot numbers and certificates, and the technician identification are all stated, and photographs are labeled with the weld number and date. If your plant needs a particular template, tell us when you request the quotation.

Records are retained in line with the contract, and the owner decides how long it needs them. For equipment that falls under a state boiler and pressure vessel inspection or an insurer's program, the report is available to the inspector who visits next, which avoids repeating the examination simply because the earlier result cannot be found.

Codes and acceptance

The method is covered by ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 for general industrial use. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 where penetrant testing is allowed on structural welds, and the customer's own specification for castings and machined parts. Our Article 6 guide explains the controls.

Some aerospace and defense production parts require special-process approvals that Atlantis does not hold, so this service is aimed at industrial plant equipment and general fabrication. In Missouri, the Division of Fire Safety enforces the state boiler and pressure vessel law, with certificate inspections the owner's responsibility; where API 510 or API 570 applies, the owner's authorized inspector directs the work and Atlantis reports the surface indications.

Personnel and reporting

A Level II technician qualified under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, performs the test and interprets indications. An ASNT Level III reviews the report and approves the procedure, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. SNT-TC-1A gives the employer the job of certifying personnel, so a buyer should ask to see the written practice.

The report records the part and its identification, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with lot numbers, cleaning method, dwell and development times, temperature, lighting, technician and level, and the date. Each indication is described by type, position and size, with a photograph or sketch, and accepted or rejected against the named table. Parts re-examined after repair are listed with both results.

Planning a penetrant job in St. Louis

Humid summers can slow evaporation of solvent cleaners and make fluorescent examination uncomfortable in a closed booth, and cold winters put shop floors and outdoor pipe racks below the qualified temperature range. Plan heat, enclosure or a procedure qualified for the temperature in use. Penetrant materials should be stored where they stay within their temperature limits, and developer needs still air to lay down evenly.

Atlantis has no office in St. Louis, so technicians travel to your site; the quotation covers the agreed scope and travel. At chemical, brewing and pharmaceutical sites, tell us about hygiene rules, material approvals and permitted chemicals in advance, since penetrant products may need to be cleared before they enter the plant. Send the part list, material, surface condition and code for a quotation.

Which method fits: PT, MT or UT in St. Louis

Penetrant suits non-magnetic metals and any surface-breaking flaw on non-porous material. For carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in St. Louis is usually faster. For internal flaws and remaining wall, use ultrasonic testing in St. Louis. The MT versus PT comparison and the national penetrant testing page give more detail.

Training in-house penetrant technicians

Employers who want to qualify their own staff can use PT Level 1 training, PT Level 2 training and the penetrant simulator. See the St. Louis training page for the format; your employer remains the certifying party under its written practice.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in St. Louis for penetrant testing?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in St. Louis. Technicians are mobilized to your plant or shop with the penetrant system, lighting and procedure, and the quotation includes travel for the agreed scope.

faq.q: Can dye penetrant find cracks in aluminum castings?
faq.a: Yes, if the crack is open to the surface. Fluorescent penetrant is usually chosen for aluminum castings because it shows fine cracks on rough surfaces. Buried shrinkage or porosity needs a different method.

faq.q: Why can grinding or blasting cause missed cracks?
faq.a: These processes can smear or peen metal across a crack mouth and seal it, so penetrant cannot enter. The procedure may call for etching or a different cleaning method before penetrant, particularly on soft alloys.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 uses 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the temperature actually used, which matters on cold shop floors and hot summer surfaces.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible penetrant is a colored dye read in white light and is easy to use in the field. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light and is more sensitive, so it is used on castings and critical parts.

faq.q: Is penetrant safe to use on stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes, with materials certified for low halogen and sulfur content, and with residues removed after the test. The report lists the materials and lots so the owner can verify they met the specification.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing tell how deep a crack is?
faq.a: No. It shows only the surface opening. Depth is estimated with ultrasonic testing, or established by grinding and re-examining. The report records length and position of each indication.

faq.q: What does a penetrant report include?
faq.a: The part ID, procedure, penetrant system and lots, cleaning, dwell and development times, temperature, lighting, technician and level, and each indication with location, size and accept or reject against the named code.

faq.q: How do I request penetrant testing in St. Louis?
faq.a: Use the quote form with the part list, material, surface condition, governing code and preferred dates. We reply within one business day with a scope and a written quotation.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing St. Louis, MO | UT Alternatives
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. In St. Louis, MO we offer UT as a volumetric alternative, Level III image review and RT theory training.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in St. Louis, Missouri
rt.html:
Radiographic testing is not a service Atlantis performs in the United States. Industrial radiography is licensed: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission governs it under 10 CFR Part 34, and Agreement States apply equivalent rules. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in St. Louis or anywhere else in this country. If you came to this page looking for RT, here is what Atlantis can do for you.

Ultrasonic testing where the code allows a volumetric substitute

For some weld examinations, ultrasonic testing is an accepted route to the same answer radiography gives, which is whether the inside of the weld is sound. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 sets ultrasonic acceptance for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only where specific conditions are met. That is a decision for the owner, the engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector, made before the job.

Atlantis technicians are mobilized to St. Louis sites for ultrasonic weld and thickness examination; read about ultrasonic testing in St. Louis or ask for a UT quote to find out whether it fits the welds you have.

Reviewing radiographs and radiography procedures

A radiography contractor produces images; somebody has to judge them. Atlantis's ASNT Level III can examine radiographs, whether film or digital files, together with technique sheets and image quality indicator results against Article 2 of ASME Section V and the governing construction code. Owners ask for this when two readers disagree about an indication, when a weld repair is under dispute, or when they want a check on a contractor's procedure and written practice before accepting its work.

The review is led by our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. No radiation source is involved, so no licence is needed for the review itself. We do not recommend or name radiography contractors. For the broader service, see Level III consulting and written practice development.

Radiography theory instruction

An employer building its own radiography capability can use Atlantis for the classroom part of the program. The radiographic testing Level 2 course covers the theory behind the method. Practical exposure work, radiation safety training and licensing stay with the licensee and the regulator, and the employer certifies its own technicians under its written practice. The St. Louis training page has more on formats.

Other options for St. Louis owners

If the real need behind the search is a surface crack or a wall measurement, other methods fit more directly: magnetic particle inspection in St. Louis for carbon steel and liquid penetrant testing in St. Louis for non-magnetic metals. Atlantis has no office in St. Louis, so technicians travel to your site. Tell us what you need to learn about the weld or casting, and we will say which method answers it, including when a licensed radiography contractor is the right choice.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do X-ray inspection of welds in St. Louis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography requires a licence under NRC rules or an Agreement State's equivalent. We offer ultrasonic examination and Level III review of images instead.

faq.q: When can ultrasonic testing be used in place of radiography?
faq.a: Only when the construction code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it under set conditions. Agree it with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can I get a second opinion on radiographs from another company?
faq.a: Yes. Our Level III can read film or digital images with the technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and give an independent opinion on disputed indications.

faq.q: Do you recommend radiography contractors in the St. Louis area?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. If you need radiography, choose a licensed contractor of your own; we can review its procedure or images independently.

faq.q: Is there radiography training available through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes, theory instruction is available through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Practical exposure, radiation safety and licensing remain with the licensee, and the employer certifies technicians under its written practice.
